title: Διὸς ἔγερσις
about: Zeus wakes on Ida to find the Trojans in flight and Hector lying half-conscious, spitting blood, with Poseidon helping the Achaeans. He turns on Hera, whose trick put him to sleep, and reminds her of the day he hung her in the sky with anvils on her feet. Frightened, Hera swears by the Styx that Poseidon acts on his own. Zeus relaxes and tells her to summon Iris and Apollo: Poseidon is to leave the fight, and Apollo is to revive Hector and rout the Achaeans. He foretells what follows: Patroclus will fight, Sarpedon will fall, Hector will kill Patroclus and Achilles will kill Hector, and Troy will fall. Hera flies to Olympus, where the gods rise to greet her and Themis asks what has frightened her.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ διά τε σκόλοπας καὶ τάφρον ἔβησαν
φεύγοντες, πολλοὶ δὲ δάμεν Δαναῶν ὑπὸ χερσίν,
οἳ μὲν δὴ παρ’ ὄχεσφιν ἐρητύοντο μένοντες
χλωροὶ ὑπαὶ δείους πεφοβημένοι·
sentences.l:
But when through both the stakes and the ditch they had gone,
fleeing, and many were subdued by the hands of the Danaans,
these by their chariots were held back, staying,
pale beneath fear, frightened;
sentences.i: But when they had gone in flight through the stakes and the ditch, and many had been laid low at the hands of the Danaans, these were held back at their chariots, staying there, pale with fear and frightened;
sentences.n: The fugitives are the Trojans, not named until line 6: they have fled back over the Achaean ditch and stakes, and many fell to Danaan hands on the way. The first line and a half repeat 8.343–344, with Δαναῶν ‘of the Danaans’ where that line has Τρώων. οἳ μὲν δή ‘these, indeed’ is answered by ἔγρετο δὲ Ζεύς in the next unit. ἐρητύοντο is an imperfect passive of ἐρητύω ‘hold back’; ὄχεσφιν has the epic ending -φιν, ‘chariots’. πεφοβημένοι is the perfect passive participle of φοβέω ‘frighten, put to flight’.

sentences.t:
ἔγρετο δὲ Ζεὺς
Ἴδης ἐν κορυφῇσι παρὰ χρυσοθρόνου Ἥρης,
sentences.l:
and awoke Zeus
on the peaks of Ida, beside golden-throned Hera,
sentences.i: Zeus awoke on the peaks of Ida, beside golden-throned Hera;
sentences.n: ἔγρετο, the aorist of ἐγείρω in the middle, means ‘awoke’: Zeus has been asleep since Hera’s deception in Book 14, and now the poem turns on his waking. Ἴδης ἐν κορυφῇσι is ‘on the peaks of Ida’, the mountain above Troy. Ἥρης is the Ionic genitive of Ἥρα. χρυσόθρονος is the stock epithet of Hera, ‘golden-throned’ (θρόνος ‘seat’); some ancient readers took the first part as θρόνα ‘flowers’, so the formation is not certain.

sentences.t:
στῆ δ’ ἄρ’ ἀναΐξας, ἴδε δὲ Τρῶας καὶ Ἀχαιοὺς
τοὺς μὲν ὀρινομένους, τοὺς δὲ κλονέοντας ὄπισθεν
Ἀργείους, μετὰ δέ σφι Ποσειδάωνα ἄνακτα·
sentences.i: He sprang up and stood, and saw the Trojans and the Achaeans, some thrown into turmoil and others, the Argives, throwing them into confusion from behind, and lord Poseidon among them;
sentences.n: τοὺς μέν … τοὺς δέ ‘some … others’ splits the two armies: the Trojans are ὀρινομένους ‘stirred up, thrown into turmoil’, and Ἀργείους, in apposition to the second group, are κλονέοντας ‘throwing them into confusion’ from behind; Achaeans and Argives are one army under two names. Line 7 is 14.14 with ὄπισθεν for ὄπισθε. ἀναΐξας is the aorist participle of ἀναΐσσω ‘spring up’, and στῆ the unaugmented ‘he stood’. μετὰ δέ σφι ‘and among them’: σφι is the epic dative plural; Ποσειδάωνα ἄνακτα is ‘lord Poseidon’.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορα δ’ ἐν πεδίῳ ἴδε κείμενον, ἀμφὶ δ’ ἑταῖροι
εἵαθ’, ὃ δ’ ἀργαλέῳ ἔχετ’ ἄσθματι κῆρ ἀπινύσσων
αἷμ’ ἐμέων, ἐπεὶ οὔ μιν ἀφαυρότατος βάλ’ Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l:
And Hector on the plain he saw lying, and around him his companions
sat, and he by grievous gasping was held, lacking sense at heart,
vomiting blood, since not him the weakest of the Achaeans had struck.
sentences.i: He saw Hector lying on the plain, with his companions sitting around him, and Hector was held in grievous gasping, lacking sense at heart, and vomiting blood, since it was not the weakest of the Achaeans who had struck him.
sentences.n: This is Hector as Book 14 left him, struck down by Ajax’s stone. εἵαθ’ is εἵατο, the imperfect of ἧμαι ‘sit’; ἔχετ’ is ἔχετο, ‘was held’, with the dative ἀργαλέῳ ἄσθματι ‘in grievous gasping’ saying what held him. κῆρ is an accusative of respect, ‘in heart’, with ἀπινύσσων, ‘lacking sense’ (from the root of πινυτός ‘sensible’). ἐμέων is the uncontracted participle of ἐμέω ‘vomit’. βάλ’ is the unaugmented ἔβαλε. οὔ μιν ἀφαυρότατος … ‘not the weakest’: a way of saying that a strong man struck him.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ ἰδὼν ἐλέησε πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε,
δεινὰ δ’ ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν Ἥρην πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν·
sentences.l:
And him seeing, pitied the father of men and of gods,
and dreadfully, with a scowl looking at Hera, he addressed her with a word:
sentences.i: The father of men and of gods pitied him when he saw him, and, looking at Hera with a dreadful scowl, spoke to her:
sentences.n: The ‘father of men and of gods’ is Zeus, unnamed here and translated in full every time. τὸν δὲ ἰδών ‘and seeing him’ gives ἐλέησε ‘pitied’ its object, Hector. ὑπόδρα ‘with a scowl’ is an adverb for a look from under the brows; its derivation is not certain. δεινά, the neuter plural used as an adverb, is ‘dreadfully’. Ἥρην is the object of ἰδών. πρὸς … ἔειπεν is tmesis for ‘addressed’, with μῦθον ‘a word’ as the object; ἔειπεν is the aorist of εἶπον with the epic doubled ε. The edition prints no quotation marks, so the speech begins with the next line.

sentences.t:
ἦ μάλα δὴ κακότεχνος ἀμήχανε σὸς δόλος Ἥρη
Ἕκτορα δῖον ἔπαυσε μάχης, ἐφόβησε δὲ λαούς.
sentences.l:
“Truly, very much so, evil-crafted, you who are past all dealing with, your trick, Hera,
has stopped heavenly Hector from battle, and put the people to flight.
sentences.i: “Surely, Hera, you who are impossible to deal with, your evil-crafted trick has stopped heavenly Hector from battle and put the people to flight.
sentences.n: Zeus begins with an accusation. κακότεχνος ‘evil-crafted’ goes with σὸς δόλος ‘your trick’; ἀμήχανε is a vocative, ‘you who are past all dealing with’ (ἀμήχανος, ‘without resource’, of someone no device can manage), and Ἥρη, at the end of the line, is a second vocative. ἔπαυσε μάχης takes the genitive of what is stopped, ‘stopped from battle’. ἐφόβησε is the aorist of φοβέω ‘put to flight’, and λαούς ‘the people’ are the Trojan army. The ‘trick’ is Hera’s seduction and the sleep of Zeus in Book 14.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὰν οἶδ’ εἰ αὖτε κακορραφίης ἀλεγεινῆς
πρώτη ἐπαύρηαι καί σε πληγῇσιν ἱμάσσω.
sentences.l:
Truly I do not know whether again of grievous ill-contriving
you will be the first to have the benefit, and I lash you with blows.
sentences.i: I truly do not know whether you will once more be the first to have the benefit of your grievous bad planning, and I lash you with blows.
sentences.n: A threat. οὐ μὰν οἶδα ‘truly I do not know’ opens an indirect question with εἰ ‘whether’ and two subjunctives, ἐπαύρηαι and ἱμάσσω: ‘whether you will have the benefit … and I lash you’. ἐπαύρηαι, from ἐπαυρίσκομαι, takes the genitive and means ‘have the benefit of’, bitterly ironic here, since the benefit will be a beating. κακορραφίη, ‘ill-contriving, bad planning’, is built on κακά and ῥάπτω ‘stitch’. πληγῇσιν is the epic dative plural of πληγή ‘blow’; ἱμάσσω comes from ἱμάς ‘thong’, ‘lash’.

sentences.l:
Do you not remember when you hung from on high, and from your feet
two anvils I let down, and around your hands a bond I cast,
golden, unbreakable?
sentences.i: Do you not remember when you hung from on high, and I let two anvils down from your feet and cast a golden bond, unbreakable, around your hands?
sentences.n: Zeus recalls an old punishment of Hera, which he assumes she remembers. μέμνῃ is μέμνηαι, a perfect with present sense, ‘you remember’; ἐκρέμω is the imperfect of κρέμαμαι ‘hang’, and ὑψόθεν is ‘from on high’. ποδοῖιν is an epic dual, ‘from both feet’. ἧκα is the aorist of ἵημι, here ‘let down’, and ἴηλα the aorist of ἰάλλω ‘send, cast’ (the Odyssey has ἴηλον in the same use). ἄρρηκτον ‘unbreakable’ and χρύσεον ‘golden’ qualify δεσμόν ‘bond’. The unit ends at the Greek question mark.

sentences.t:
σὺ δ’ ἐν αἰθέρι καὶ νεφέλῃσιν
ἐκρέμω·
sentences.l:
and you in the upper air and the clouds
were hanging;
sentences.i: and you hung there in the upper air and in the clouds;
sentences.n: ἐν αἰθέρι καὶ νεφέλῃσιν ‘in the upper air and the clouds’ says where she hung: αἰθήρ is the bright upper sky, and νεφέλῃσιν is the epic dative plural of νεφέλη ‘cloud’. ἐκρέμω, the second-person imperfect middle of κρέμαμαι, repeats the verb of the question just before, now as a plain statement, and the ano teleia sets the picture apart.

sentences.t:
ἠλάστεον δὲ θεοὶ κατὰ μακρὸν Ὄλυμπον,
λῦσαι δ’ οὐκ ἐδύναντο παρασταδόν·
sentences.l:
and the gods were in bitter indignation throughout tall Olympus,
but to loose you they were not able, standing beside you;
sentences.i: and the gods throughout tall Olympus were in bitter indignation, but could not free you, though they stood beside you;
sentences.n: ἠλάστεον is the imperfect of ἀλαστέω ‘be in bitter indignation’, from the root of ἄλαστος ‘not to be forgotten’; the exact force is not certain. κατὰ μακρὸν Ὄλυμπον is ‘throughout tall Olympus’. λῦσαι, the aorist infinitive of λύω, has no object stated; ‘you’ carries over from the clauses before. ἐδύναντο is the imperfect of δύναμαι, with the epic augment ἐ- where Attic usually has ἠ-. παρασταδόν is an adverb in -δόν, ‘standing beside’ (παρίστημι).

sentences.t:
ὃν δὲ λάβοιμι
ῥίπτασκον τεταγὼν ἀπὸ βηλοῦ ὄφρ’ ἂν ἵκηται
γῆν ὀλιγηπελέων·
sentences.i: and whomever I caught I would seize and fling from the threshold, until he reached the earth, faint;
sentences.n: ὃν δὲ λάβοιμι is a general condition in the past, ‘whomever I caught’, with the optative; ῥίπτασκον carries the iterative suffix -σκ-, ‘I would fling’, as a repeated act. τεταγών is an old reduplicated aorist participle, ‘seizing’. ἀπὸ βηλοῦ ‘from the threshold’ (of heaven) echoes Hephaestus’ account of his own throwing at 1.591. ὄφρ’ ἂν ἵκηται is ‘until he reached’, with ἄν and the subjunctive. ὀλιγηπελέων is ‘faint with little strength’.

sentences.t:
ἐμὲ δ’ οὐδ’ ὧς θυμὸν ἀνίει
ἀζηχὴς ὀδύνη Ἡρακλῆος θείοιο,
sentences.l:
but me not even so, as to my heart, did it let go,
the incessant pain for Heracles, divine one,
sentences.i: but even so the incessant pain for divine Heracles did not let go of my heart,
sentences.n: ἐμὲ … θυμόν is ‘me, as to my heart’, a person and the part affected both in the accusative. ἀνίει is the imperfect of ἀνίημι ‘let go, release’, and its subject comes last, ἀζηχὴς ὀδύνη ‘incessant pain’; ἀζηχής is of uncertain origin and ‘unceasing’ is the traditional sense. Ἡρακλῆος θείοιο is a genitive, ‘for Heracles’, with θεῖος ‘divine’ (a different word from δῖος ‘heavenly’). Zeus’s grief for his son was not eased even by punishing Hera. The sentence runs on into the next unit.

sentences.t:
τὸν σὺ ξὺν Βορέῃ ἀνέμῳ πεπιθοῦσα θυέλλας
πέμψας ἐπ’ ἀτρύγετον πόντον κακὰ μητιόωσα,
καί μιν ἔπειτα Κόων δ’ εὖ ναιομένην ἀπένεικας.
sentences.l:
whom you, with the North Wind, having persuaded the storm-blasts,
having sent over the unharvested open-sea, devising evils,
and him then to well-inhabited Cos you carried away.
sentences.i: whom you, having persuaded the storm-blasts together with the North Wind, sent out over the sea that yields no harvest, devising evil, and then carried him off to well-inhabited Cos.
sentences.n: The relative τόν ‘whom’ (Heracles) is taken up again by μιν ‘him’ in line 28, so the sentence begins as a relative clause and ends as a main clause. πεπιθοῦσα is a reduplicated aorist participle of πείθω ‘persuade’; the usual reading takes θυέλλας ‘storm-blasts’ as its object and τόν as the object of πέμψας ‘sent’, with ξὺν Βορέῃ ἀνέμῳ ‘together with the North Wind’ making Boreas her ally. The construction is loose, and θυέλλας could instead be the object of πέμψας. ἀτρύγετον is traditionally ‘unharvested’, though the word’s sense is not actually known. Κόων δ’ is ‘to Cos’ (-δε marks direction). Line 28 is 14.255.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἐγὼν ἔνθεν ῥυσάμην καὶ ἀνήγαγον αὖτις
Ἄργος ἐς ἱππόβοτον καὶ πολλά περ ἀθλήσαντα.
sentences.l:
Him I from there rescued and brought back up again
to horse-pasturing Argos, even though he had laboured much.
sentences.i: I rescued him from there and brought him back again to horse-pasturing Argos, for all that he had toiled much.
sentences.n: τὸν μέν ‘him’ is Heracles; ἐγών is the epic form of ἐγώ; ἔνθεν is ‘from there’, from Cos. ῥυσάμην is the aorist middle of ῥύομαι ‘rescue, protect’, and ἀνήγαγον the aorist of ἀνάγω ‘lead up, bring back’, with αὖτις ‘again’ (Attic αὖθις). ἱππόβοτος ‘horse-pasturing’ is built on βόσκω ‘pasture’. πολλά περ ἀθλήσαντα is concessive, ‘though he had toiled much’: ἀθλέω ‘toil, labour’ points to the labours of Heracles.

sentences.t:
τῶν σ’ αὖτις μνήσω ἵν’ ἀπολλήξῃς ἀπατάων,
ὄφρα ἴδῃ ἤν τοι χραίσμῃ φιλότης τε καὶ εὐνή,
ἣν ἐμίγης ἐλθοῦσα θεῶν ἄπο καί μ’ ἀπάτησας.
sentences.l:
Of these things again I will remind you, that you may cease from deceits,
so that you may see if for you will avail love and the bed,
in which you were mingled, having come from the gods apart, and deceived me.”
sentences.i: I shall remind you of these things again, so that you may stop your deceits, and may see whether love and the bed will help you, in which you lay with me when you came away from the gods and deceived me.”
sentences.n: τῶν ‘of these things’ is a genitive after μνήσω, the future of μιμνῄσκω in its causative sense ‘I will remind’ (person accusative, thing genitive). ἀπολλήξῃς ἀπατάων is ‘you may cease from deceits’: ἀπολλήγω takes the genitive, and ἀπατάων is the epic genitive plural of ἀπάτη. ὄφρα ἴδῃ is printed as it stands; the sense needs ‘you may see’, read as second person. ἤν is εἰ ἄν ‘if’, and χραίσμῃ is an aorist subjunctive of χραισμέω ‘help’. ἐμίγης is the aorist passive of μείγνυμι, ‘you were mingled’; ἣν, feminine accusative, refers to φιλότης or εὐνή, ‘in which’, and ‘me’ is supplied in the English. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, ῥίγησεν δὲ βοῶπις πότνια Ἥρη,
καί μιν φωνήσασ’ ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and shuddered ox-eyed lady Hera,
and, lifting her voice, to him winged words she spoke:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and ox-eyed lady Hera shuddered, and, raising her voice, spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: The threat has frightened her: ῥίγησεν, the aorist of ῥιγέω, is the shudder of fear. βοῶπις ‘ox-eyed’ is the stock epithet of Hera; the usual explanation is large, calm eyes, and πότνια is ‘lady’. The second line is the formula that opens a speech: φωνήσασα ‘raising her voice’, ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’ (the picture is of words flying from speaker to hearer), προσηύδα ‘spoke to’, and μιν ‘him’, Zeus. Both are translated every time in the same way. She answers with an oath.

sentences.t:
ἴστω νῦν τόδε Γαῖα καὶ Οὐρανὸς εὐρὺς ὕπερθε
καὶ τὸ κατειβόμενον Στυγὸς ὕδωρ, ὅς τε μέγιστος
ὅρκος δεινότατός τε πέλει μακάρεσσι θεοῖσι,
sentences.l:
“Let now the earth know this, and the wide sky above,
and the down-flowing water of the Styx, which is the greatest
oath and the most dread for the blessed gods,
sentences.i: “Now let the earth know this, and the wide sky above, and the down-flowing water of the Styx, which is the greatest and most dread oath for the blessed gods,
sentences.n: An oath, and its form is the Odyssey’s: lines 36–38 are Calypso’s oath at Odyssey 5.184–186, with the same English. ἴστω, the imperative of οἶδα, is literally ‘let know’; as an oath it means ‘let be witness’. Γαῖα ‘Earth’ and Οὐρανός ‘Sky’ are called on as gods, and so is the Styx, whose water is the oath that binds the gods most. κατειβόμενον is ‘down-flowing’; ὅς τε μέγιστος ὅρκος … πέλει is ‘which is the greatest oath’, with δεινότατος ‘most dread’ and μακάρεσσι θεοῖσι ‘for the blessed gods’. The oath goes on in the next unit, and its content comes at line 41.

sentences.t:
σή θ’ ἱερὴ κεφαλὴ καὶ νωΐτερον λέχος αὐτῶν
κουρίδιον, τὸ μὲν οὐκ ἂν ἐγώ ποτε μὰψ ὀμόσαιμι·
sentences.l:
and your sacred head, and the bed of us two, our very own,
wedded, this at least I would never at any time swear recklessly;
sentences.i: and your sacred head, and our own wedded bed, the bed of us two: that oath I would never swear recklessly;
sentences.n: Two more things she swears by. σή is ‘your’, and ἱερὴ κεφαλή ‘sacred head’ puts the head for the person. νωΐτερον is the possessive of νῶϊ ‘we two’, ‘belonging to us two’, and αὐτῶν adds ‘ourselves’: the bed is theirs alone. κουρίδιον is ‘wedded’, of lawful marriage. τὸ μέν, ‘this one at least’, is the oath by the bed, which she says she would never swear μάψ ‘recklessly’; ὀμόσαιμι is an aorist optative, with οὐκ ἂν ‘would not’, and ποτε adds ‘ever’.

sentences.t:
μὴ δι’ ἐμὴν ἰότητα Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων
πημαίνει Τρῶάς τε καὶ Ἕκτορα, τοῖσι δ’ ἀρήγει,
ἀλλά που αὐτὸν θυμὸς ἐποτρύνει καὶ ἀνώγει,
τειρομένους δ’ ἐπὶ νηυσὶν ἰδὼν ἐλέησεν Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.l:
that not through my will does Poseidon earth-shaker
harm the Trojans and Hector, and give help to those;
but doubtless his own heart urges him and bids,
and, seeing the Achaeans being worn down at the ships, he pitied them.
sentences.i: that it is not through any will of mine that Poseidon the earth-shaker harms the Trojans and Hector and helps those others; but doubtless his own heart urges and bids him, and he pitied the Achaeans when he saw them worn down at the ships.
sentences.n: This is what she swears: μή … πημαίνει ‘that not … does he harm’, the negative of a sworn statement, with διὰ ἐμὴν ἰότητα ‘through my will’. πημαίνω ‘harm’ is built on πῆμα ‘woe’; ἀρήγει ‘helps’ takes the dative τοῖσι ‘those’, the other side, who are named only in line 44. Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων is ‘Poseidon the earth-shaker’. ἀλλά που is ‘but doubtless’; αὐτόν is the object ‘him’ and θυμός the subject, ‘his own heart’ in English. τειρομένους is the passive participle of τείρω ‘wear down’, and ἐλέησεν the aorist ‘pitied’. Hera says Poseidon acts on his own.

sentences.t:
αὐτάρ τοι καὶ κείνῳ ἐγὼ παραμυθησαίμην
τῇ ἴμεν ᾗ κεν δὴ σὺ κελαινεφὲς ἡγεμονεύῃς.
sentences.l:
But, I tell you, to that one too I would give counsel
to go by that way by which you, dark-clouded one, may lead.”
sentences.i: But I would advise even him to go the way that you, of the dark clouds, may lead.”
sentences.n: She ends by offering to bring Poseidon round. παραμυθησαίμην is an aorist optative, ‘I would counsel’ (παραμυθέομαι ‘speak to, urge’); the optative without ἄν makes it a polite offer. καὶ κείνῳ ‘even him’ is Poseidon, who is not named; κεῖνος is the Ionic form of ἐκεῖνος. τοι means ‘I tell you’. τῇ … ᾗ is ‘by that way … by which’, ἴμεν is the epic infinitive of εἶμι ‘go’, and ἡγεμονεύῃς, with κεν, is ‘you may lead’. κελαινεφές is the vocative of κελαινεφής ‘dark-clouded’, a title of Zeus as the gatherer of storm-clouds. Her speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, μείδησεν δὲ πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε,
καί μιν ἀμειβόμενος ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
So she spoke, and smiled the father of men and of gods,
and, answering her, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: So she spoke, and the father of men and of gods smiled, and in answer to her spoke winged words:
sentences.n: Zeus smiles: her oath has pleased him. The first line is a formula the poem uses again, with the same speaker, at 5.426 (to Aphrodite). μείδησεν is the aorist of μειδάω ‘smile’. The unnamed ‘father of men and of gods’ is Zeus. ἀμειβόμενος is the participle of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’, with μιν ‘her’; ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the speech formula again, ‘winged words he spoke to her’.

sentences.t:
εἰ μὲν δὴ σύ γ’ ἔπειτα βοῶπις πότνια Ἥρη
ἶσον ἐμοὶ φρονέουσα μετ’ ἀθανάτοισι καθίζοις,
τώ κε Ποσειδάων γε, καὶ εἰ μάλα βούλεται ἄλλῃ,
αἶψα μεταστρέψειε νόον μετὰ σὸν καὶ ἐμὸν κῆρ.
sentences.l:
“If indeed you, from now on, ox-eyed lady Hera,
thinking equally with me, among the immortals would sit,
then Poseidon, even if he very much wishes otherwise,
at once would turn his mind after your heart and mine.
sentences.i: “If from now on you, ox-eyed lady Hera, would sit among the immortals thinking just as I do, then Poseidon, even if he very much wishes it otherwise, would at once turn his mind to follow your heart and mine.
sentences.n: A conditional about what he hopes for, not what is so: εἰ with the optative καθίζοις, ‘if you would sit’, answered by κε with the optative μεταστρέψειε, ‘he would turn’. ἔπειτα is ‘from now on’. ἶσον ἐμοὶ φρονέουσα is ‘thinking equally with me’. τώ is ‘then, in that case’. ἄλλῃ, a dative used as an adverb, is ‘otherwise’. μετά with the accusative σὸν καὶ ἐμὸν κῆρ means ‘after, to follow your heart and mine’; νόος is ‘mind’ (Attic νοῦς), and αἶψα is ‘at once’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ εἰ δή ῥ’ ἐτεόν γε καὶ ἀτρεκέως ἀγορεύεις,
ἔρχεο νῦν μετὰ φῦλα θεῶν, καὶ δεῦρο κάλεσσον
Ἶρίν τ’ ἐλθέμεναι καὶ Ἀπόλλωνα κλυτότοξον,
sentences.l:
But if indeed truly and exactly you speak,
go now among the tribes of the gods, and call here
Iris to come and Apollo famed-for-the-bow,
sentences.i: But if you really mean this, and are saying it exactly, go now among the tribes of the gods, and call Iris here to come, and Apollo, famed for his bow,
sentences.n: The plan begins. ἀλλ’ εἰ δή ‘but if indeed’ has ἐτεόν ‘really’ and ἀτρεκέως ‘exactly’ both going with ἀγορεύεις ‘you speak’. ἔρχεο is the imperative of ἔρχομαι ‘go’, and φῦλα are ‘tribes’ of the gods. κάλεσσον is the aorist imperative of καλέω, with the doubled σσ, and ἐλθέμεναι the epic infinitive ‘to come’. Ἶρις and Ἀπόλλων are the two messengers. κλυτότοξος is ‘famed for the bow’ (κλυτός ‘famous’, τόξον ‘bow’), a stock epithet of Apollo.

sentences.t:
ὄφρ’ ἣ μὲν μετὰ λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων
ἔλθῃ, καὶ εἴπῃσι Ποσειδάωνι ἄνακτι
παυσάμενον πολέμοιο τὰ ἃ πρὸς δώμαθ’ ἱκέσθαι,
sentences.l:
so that she, on the one hand, among the host of the bronze-shirted Achaeans
may go, and say to Poseidon the lord
that, having ceased from war, he is to come to his own halls,
sentences.i: so that she may go among the host of the bronze-shirted Achaeans and tell lord Poseidon to stop the war and go to his own halls,
sentences.n: A run of ὄφρα ‘so that’ clauses with subjunctives lays out the plan, divided between two messengers: Iris is ἣ μέν ‘she, on the one hand’, and Apollo takes over in the next unit. εἴπῃσι is the epic subjunctive in -ῃσι. The participle παυσάμενον is in the accusative though Ποσειδάωνι ἄνακτι is a dative, as often when the subject of the infinitive ἱκέσθαι ‘to come’ is the same person: ‘tell Poseidon, having stopped, to come’. τὰ ἃ is possessive ὅς, ‘his own’, not the relative, split from δώμαθ’ (δώματα ‘halls’) by πρός. χαλκοχιτώνων is ‘bronze-shirted’.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορα δ’ ὀτρύνῃσι μάχην ἐς Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων,
αὖτις δ’ ἐμπνεύσῃσι μένος, λελάθῃ δ’ ὀδυνάων
αἳ νῦν μιν τείρουσι κατὰ φρένας,
sentences.l:
and Phoebus Apollo may rouse Hector to battle,
and again breathe might into him, and make him forget the pains
which now wear him down in his wits,
sentences.i: and Phoebus Apollo may rouse Hector to battle, and breathe might into him again, and make him forget the pains that now wear him down in his mind,
sentences.n: The second half of the plan is Apollo’s. ὀτρύνῃσι and ἐμπνεύσῃσι are subjunctives in -ῃσι, as before; μάχην ἐς is ἐς μάχην ‘to battle’ with the preposition after its noun. ἐμπνέω is ‘breathe into’, and μένος ‘might’ is the fighting power a god can put into a man. λελάθῃ is a reduplicated aorist subjunctive of λανθάνω, here causing forgetfulness, ‘make forget’, with the genitive ὀδυνάων ‘pains’; the subject is still Apollo. τείρουσι is ‘wear down’; κατὰ φρένας is ‘in his wits’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοὺς
αὖτις ἀποστρέψῃσιν ἀνάλκιδα φύζαν ἐνόρσας,
φεύγοντες δ’ ἐν νηυσὶ πολυκλήϊσι πέσωσι
Πηλεΐδεω Ἀχιλῆος·
sentences.l:
and the Achaeans
again turn back, having roused among them a panic without might,
and fleeing, among the many-thwarted ships they fall
of Peleus’-son Achilles;
sentences.i: and he may turn the Achaeans back again, rousing a panic without might among them, so that in their flight they fall among the ships of many thwarts of Peleus’ son Achilles;
sentences.n: Apollo is still the subject of ἀποστρέψῃσιν ‘may turn back’, with Ἀχαιούς as its object. φύζα is panic flight, and ἄναλκις ‘without might’ describes a flight in which no one stands to fight; ἐνόρσας is the aorist participle of ἐνόρνυμι ‘rouse in’. The subject then changes: φεύγοντες ‘fleeing’ is the Achaeans, who are the subject of πέσωσι, the aorist subjunctive of πίπτω. πολυκλήϊσι is the stock epithet of ships, ‘many-thwarted’ (κληΐς is a thwart, a rowers’ bench). Πηλεΐδεω is a patronymic with the epic genitive -εω, ‘of Peleus’ son’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἀνστήσει ὃν ἑταῖρον
Πάτροκλον·
sentences.l:
and he will rouse his own companion
Patroclus;
sentences.i: and he will rouse his own companion Patroclus;
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘and he’ is Achilles, with the old pronoun that is turning into the article. ἀνστήσει is the future of ἀνίστημι in its transitive sense ‘make rise, rouse’, a shortened form of ἀναστήσει; the sense is ‘rouse to the fight’. ὃν ἑταῖρον is the possessive ὅς ‘his own’ with ἑταῖρος ‘companion’. Zeus now foretells, one step after another, what the poem will tell: Patroclus goes out, Hector kills him, and Achilles kills Hector.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ κτενεῖ ἔγχεϊ φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ
Ἰλίου προπάροιθε πολέας ὀλέσαντ’ αἰζηοὺς
τοὺς ἄλλους, μετὰ δ’ υἱὸν ἐμὸν Σαρπηδόνα δῖον.
sentences.l:
and him will kill with a spear glorious Hector
before Ilios, after he has destroyed many vigorous men,
the others, and among them my son, heavenly Sarpedon.
sentences.i: and glorious Hector will kill him with his spear before Ilios, when he has destroyed many vigorous men, the others, and among them my son, heavenly Sarpedon.
sentences.n: τὸν δέ ‘and him’ is Patroclus, and Hector is the subject of κτενεῖ, the future of κτείνω ‘kill’. ἔγχεϊ is the epic dative of ἔγχος ‘spear’. The accusative participle ὀλέσαντ’ (ὀλέσαντα) agrees with τόν, Patroclus, not with Hector: it is Patroclus who will have destroyed many. Ἰλίου προπάροιθε is ‘before Ilios’, and αἰζηοί are vigorous men in their prime. τοὺς ἄλλους is ‘the others’, and μετά is adverbial: Sarpedon, Zeus’s own son, is counted among them, though he is named last. φαίδιμος ‘glorious’ and δῖος ‘heavenly’ are stock epithets.

sentences.t: τοῦ δὲ χολωσάμενος κτενεῖ Ἕκτορα δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς.
sentences.l: And angered on his account, will kill Hector heavenly Achilles.
sentences.i: And in anger for his sake heavenly Achilles will kill Hector.
sentences.n: The last step of the chain. τοῦ ‘his’ is Patroclus, a genitive of the person on whose account Achilles is angry; χολωσάμενος is the aorist participle of χολόομαι ‘be angered’, from χόλος ‘anger’. κτενεῖ is the same future as in line 65, now with Hector as its object (Ἕκτορα) and Achilles as its subject. δῖος ‘heavenly’ is the stock epithet. The unit stands alone because it ends at the full stop.

sentences.t:
ἐκ τοῦ δ’ ἄν τοι ἔπειτα παλίωξιν παρὰ νηῶν
αἰὲν ἐγὼ τεύχοιμι διαμπερὲς εἰς ὅ κ’ Ἀχαιοὶ
Ἴλιον αἰπὺ ἕλοιεν Ἀθηναίης διὰ βουλάς.
sentences.l:
And from that time on, I tell you, a chase back from the ships
always I would keep making, right through, until the Achaeans
steep Ilios might take, through the counsels of Athena.
sentences.i: From that time on I would always keep up a chase back from the ships, right through, until the Achaeans take steep Ilios through the counsels of Athena.
sentences.n: Zeus says what he himself will do. ἐκ τοῦ is ‘from that (time)’, from Hector’s death. παλίωξις, ‘a chase back’, is a rare word and its sense is not exactly known; it is taken here as the Trojans being driven back from the ships. ἄν … τεύχοιμι is an optative with ἄν, ‘I would make’; τοι adds ‘I tell you’. εἰς ὅ κ’ … ἕλοιεν is ‘until they take’ (optative after εἰς ὅ κε), with αἰὲν ‘always’ and διαμπερές ‘right through’. Ἴλιον αἰπύ is ‘steep Ilios’. Ἀθηναίης διὰ βουλάς is ‘through the counsels of Athena’, διά with the accusative meaning ‘thanks to’.

sentences.t:
τὸ πρὶν δ’ οὔτ’ ἄρ’ ἐγὼ παύω χόλον οὔτέ τιν’ ἄλλον
ἀθανάτων Δαναοῖσιν ἀμυνέμεν ἐνθάδ’ ἐάσω
πρίν γε τὸ Πηλεΐδαο τελευτηθῆναι ἐέλδωρ,
sentences.l:
But before that, neither will I stop my anger nor any other
of the immortals to help the Danaans here will I allow,
before the wish of Peleus’-son is accomplished,
sentences.i: But until then I will neither stop my anger nor allow any other of the immortals to help the Danaans here, before the wish of Peleus’ son is accomplished,
sentences.n: Zeus sets the one condition on which he will relent: his anger against the Danaans stays until Achilles’ wish is granted. τὸ πρὶν δέ ‘but before that’ is an adverbial phrase, and the present παύω has a future sense, ‘I will not stop’. χόλον is ‘anger’. ἀμυνέμεν is the epic infinitive of ἀμύνω ‘ward off, help’, taking the dative Δαναοῖσιν. ἐάσω is ‘I will allow’. πρίν γε with the aorist passive infinitive τελευτηθῆναι means ‘before it is accomplished’. Πηλεΐδαο is the epic genitive of Πηλεΐδης, and ἐέλδωρ is ‘wish’.

sentences.t:
ὥς οἱ ὑπέστην πρῶτον, ἐμῷ δ’ ἐπένευσα κάρητι,
ἤματι τῷ ὅτ’ ἐμεῖο θεὰ Θέτις ἥψατο γούνων,
λισσομένη τιμῆσαι Ἀχιλλῆα πτολίπορθον.
sentences.l:
as I undertook for him at first, and nodded assent with my own head,
on that day when the goddess Thetis took hold of my knees,
begging me to honour Achilles the city-sacking.”
sentences.i: as I undertook for him at the first, and nodded my assent with my own head, on the day when the goddess Thetis took hold of my knees, begging me to honour Achilles, the city-sacker.”
sentences.n: Zeus recalls the promise of Book 1, when Thetis came to him as a suppliant for her son. ὥς οἱ ὑπέστην is ‘as I undertook for him’, οἱ being Achilles, with ὑπέστην the aorist of ὑφίσταμαι. ἐπένευσα, from ἐπινεύω, is ‘I nodded assent’: Zeus’s nod is what binds. ἐμῷ κάρητι is ‘with my own head’, κάρητι an epic dative of κάρη. ἥψατο γούνων, ‘took hold of the knees’, is the suppliant’s act (ἅπτομαι with the genitive); ἐμεῖο is the epic genitive of ἐγώ. Line 77 is also 8.372, with ‘me’ for ‘him’. Zeus’s speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη,
βῆ δ’ ἐξ Ἰδαίων ὀρέων ἐς μακρὸν Ὄλυμπον.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and did not disobey, the goddess, white-armed Hera,
and went from the Idaean mountains to tall Olympus.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the goddess, white-armed Hera, did not disobey; she went from the mountains of Ida to tall Olympus.
sentences.n: Hera obeys at once. The first half-line is a formula of obedience (it stands at 5.767 with the same subject): ἔφατ’ is ‘he spoke’, and ἀπίθησε the aorist of ἀπιθέω ‘disobey’. λευκώλενος is the stock epithet ‘white-armed’. Line 79 is 8.410, where it is said of Iris: βῆ is the unaugmented ‘she went’, Ἰδαίων ὀρέων the ‘Idaean mountains’ of Ida, and μακρόν ‘tall’ the stock epithet of Olympus.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν ἀΐξῃ νόος ἀνέρος, ὅς τ’ ἐπὶ πολλὴν
γαῖαν ἐληλουθὼς φρεσὶ πευκαλίμῃσι νοήσῃ
ἔνθ’ εἴην ἢ ἔνθα, μενοινήῃσί τε πολλά,
ὣς κραιπνῶς μεμαυῖα διέπτατο πότνια Ἥρη·
sentences.l:
And as when darts forth the mind of a man who, over much
land having travelled, with keen wits thinks
of being here or there, and has many things in mind,
so at a rush, eager, flew across lady Hera;
sentences.i: As when the mind of a man darts forth, a man who has travelled over much land and in his keen wits thinks of being here or there, and has many things in mind, so, at a rush and in her eagerness, lady Hera flew across;
sentences.n: A simile for speed: nothing is quicker than a traveller’s thought, which leaps to one place or another at once. ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν ἀΐξῃ is ‘as when … darts’, a general comparison (ἀΐσσω ‘dart’). ἐληλουθώς is the perfect participle of ἔρχομαι, ‘having travelled’. νοήσῃ is ‘thinks’, and ἔνθ’ εἴην ἢ ἔνθα is ‘may I be here or there’, the wish in his mind. μενοινήῃσι is ‘has in mind’. φρεσὶ πευκαλίμῃσι is ‘keen wits’; πευκαλίμος is traditionally ‘keen’, but its formation is not certain. κραιπνῶς is ‘at a rush’, μεμαυῖα ‘eager’, and διέπτατο the aorist of διαπέτομαι ‘fly across’.

sentences.t:
ἵκετο δ’ αἰπὺν Ὄλυμπον, ὁμηγερέεσσι δ’ ἐπῆλθεν
ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσι Διὸς δόμῳ·
sentences.l:
And she came to steep Olympus, and came upon, gathered together,
the immortal gods in the house of Zeus;
sentences.i: She reached steep Olympus and came upon the immortal gods, gathered together, in the house of Zeus;
sentences.n: ἵκετο is an unaugmented past tense of ἵκω (ἱκνέομαι) ‘arrive at’. αἰπὺν Ὄλυμπον is ‘steep Olympus’, a different epithet from the μακρόν ‘tall’ of line 79. ὁμηγερέεσσι ‘gathered together’ is an epic dative plural agreeing with ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσι ‘the immortal gods’, and ἐπῆλθεν ‘came upon’ takes the dative. Διὸς δόμῳ is ‘in the house of Zeus’, where the gods meet; Zeus himself is still on Ida.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ ἰδόντες
πάντες ἀνήϊξαν καὶ δεικανόωντο δέπασσιν.
sentences.l:
and they, seeing her,
all sprang up and welcomed her with cups.
sentences.i: and when they saw her they all sprang up and welcomed her with their cups.
sentences.n: οἳ δέ ‘and they’ are the gods, and ἰδόντες ‘having seen’ has Hera understood as its object. ἀνήϊξαν is the aorist of ἀναΐσσω ‘spring up’. δεικανόωντο is the imperfect of δεικανάομαι, a rare verb of greeting, probably built on δείκνυμι ‘show, hold out’; the exact gesture is not known, and ‘welcomed … with cups’ is the usual sense. δέπασσιν is the epic dative plural of δέπας ‘cup’. The gods stand to honour her as she enters.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἄλλους μὲν ἔασε, Θέμιστι δὲ καλλιπαρῄῳ
δέκτο δέπας·
sentences.l:
And she the others let be, but from Themis, fair-cheeked,
she took the cup;
sentences.i: She let the others be, but took a cup from fair-cheeked Themis;
sentences.n: ἣ δ’ ‘and she’ is Hera. ἔασε is the aorist of ἐάω ‘let be, leave alone’. Θέμιστι is the dative of Θέμις, the goddess Themis, whose name means right custom; καλλιπαρῄῳ ‘fair-cheeked’ (παρειά ‘cheek’) is her stock epithet. δέκτο is the unaugmented aorist middle of δέχομαι ‘receive’, with the giver in the dative. Hera takes the cup from Themis alone, and the next unit says why.

sentences.t:
πρώτη γὰρ ἐναντίη ἦλθε θέουσα,
καί μιν φωνήσασ’ ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
for first she came to meet her, running,
and, lifting her voice, to her winged words she spoke:
sentences.i: for she was the first to run up and meet her, and, raising her voice, spoke winged words to her:
sentences.n: γάρ explains the choice: πρώτη ‘first’ agrees with the subject, Themis, who ἦλθε ‘came’ ἐναντίη ‘facing, to meet’ Hera and θέουσα ‘running’ (θέω). After ἦλθε the subject is still Themis, not Hera, and μιν ‘her’ is Hera. φωνήσασ’ … προσηύδα is the speech formula of line 35, now with Themis speaking. The edition prints no quotation marks, so her speech begins with the next line.

sentences.t: Ἥρη τίπτε βέβηκας;
sentences.l: “Hera, why have you come?
sentences.i: “Hera, why have you come?
sentences.n: Hera is addressed in the vocative Ἥρη. τίπτε is τί ποτε, ‘why ever’. βέβηκας is the perfect of βαίνω ‘go, step’; the perfect gives the present result, ‘you have come (and are here)’, so the question is ‘what has brought you here?’. The unit ends at the Greek question mark.

sentences.t: ἀτυζομένῃ δὲ ἔοικας·
sentences.l: and to one dazed with fear you are like;
sentences.i: You look like someone dazed with fear;
sentences.n: ἔοικας, the perfect of an old verb meaning ‘be like’, is ‘you are like, you look like’. It takes the dative participle ἀτυζομένῃ, feminine because Hera is meant: ‘like one who is dazed with fear’. ἀτύζομαι is the verb of panic that robs the wits. Themis has seen it in her face.

sentences.t: ἦ μάλα δή σ’ ἐφόβησε Κρόνου πάϊς, ὅς τοι ἀκοίτης.
sentences.l: Truly, very much so, has frightened you the son of Cronus, who is your husband.”
sentences.i: Surely it is the son of Cronus who has frightened you, he who is your husband.”
sentences.n: ἦ μάλα δή opens a confident guess, ‘surely indeed’. ἐφόβησε is the aorist of φοβέω ‘frighten’, the verb Zeus used of Hector’s people at line 15; Κρόνου πάϊς is ‘the son of Cronus’, Zeus, with πάϊς a poetic form of παῖς. ὅς τοι ἀκοίτης is ‘who is your husband’, with ‘is’ understood and τοι for σοι. Themis’ speech ends here; Hera’s answer opens the next part.
